blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: To avoid the quadratic cost of dense attention over long contexts, models such as DeepSeek-V4 and Hy4 have turned natively sparse, and speculative decoding, which matters most where decoding is slowest, increasingly runs on them. Their drafters, however, still keep a context cache of their own, over the whole prompt or a sliding window. Beyond memory, such a cache costs prefill time, prefix-cache hits and decode concurrency. Drafters that read the target's cache avoid one of their own, but settle only which cache, not which positions, and still read everything or a recent window. Neither rule is made for the query at hand, and computing a selection per query in the drafter would cost more as the context grows. Yet a natively sparse target already picks positions for each query, over a cache it keeps anyway. Both of the drafter's choices are therefore already made, and paid for, by the target: its cache and its selection. We measure how far one selection carries: made a step early, it still covers close to nine tenths of what each later token selects on DS-V4.1-Flash. We present DFly2, a block-parallel drafter that shares the target's sparsity. Each draft layer reads the KV its paired target layer cached (KV sharing), at the positions that layer's indexer selected, a fixed number anywhere in the context (Index sharing). DFly2 thus runs no scoring pass and keeps no cache of its own. On DS-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Hy4~flash, whose sparse attention and architecture differ, it accepts more tokens per step than DFlash and DSpark trained on the same recipe, over general, long-context and agentic benchmarks. Its margin over the stronger baseline widens from 3.9%-10.5% on general workloads to 10.0%-31.5% on long-context and agentic ones. At high concurrency on DS-V4.1-Flash, at matched per-user decode speed, its throughput is 62% and 81% higher on two 64K sets.

blocks.en:
Speculative decoding, a mainstream lossless accelerator, speeds up decoding further with fewer target passes,
and serving needs it most in agentic and multi-turn workloads, whose long contexts slow decoding
down ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Sadhukhan et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ) .
Long-context speculative decoding thus increasingly runs on natively sparse targets: DeepSeek-V3.2,
DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5 and Hy4 all ship with a drafter ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ; GLM-5 Team, 2026 ; Tencent Hy Team, 2026b ) .
Sparsity has made each decode step of such a target cheaper, but drafters still work in a paradigm designed
for dense targets.
We focus on block-parallel drafters, which make two choices about the target’s context: where it comes from,
meaning which cache and which positions, and how it is injected ( Chen et al., 2026 ) .
The mainstream answer takes the context from a cache of the drafter’s own, over positions picked by a rule
that ignores the current query ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Cheng et al., 2026 ; Rheinboldt et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) .
That cache holds keys and values the drafter projects from the target’s hidden states and injects into every
draft layer.
DFlash caches every position, and this cache weighs more the more the target saves ( Section 3.1 ).
It adds a fifth to the KV per token on Hy4 flash and three quarters on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
(DS-V4.1-Flash).
DSpark bounds that cost with a sliding window, which on DeepSeek-V4 spans the last 128 tokens of the
context ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) .

Drafters that read the target’s KV cache instead avoid a growing cache of their own, a line that goes back to
GliDe ( Du et al., 2024 ) and runs through LongSpec, H-Spec and LongSpark ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) .
They settle which cache to read, but not which positions.
Like DFlash and DSpark, these drafters still read every position or a recent window, by rules that ignore the
current query because the dense targets they were developed on offered no selection to follow
( Section 6 ).
Attention over all positions also grows with the context, while a fixed number of positions costs the same
at every length ( Section 3.1 ).
For drafters with a cache of their own, the better rule even depends on the target.
On long-context and agentic workloads, a full cache beats a window on DS-V4.1-Flash, loses to one on
GLM-5.3-Flash, and collapses on Hy4 flash once prompts pass the 32K the drafter was trained at
( Section 5.2 ).
A rule carried over from dense targets thus needs to be adapted to each target.
Each of these rules is fixed when the drafter is designed, not made for the query at hand, and scoring the
context instead would bring back a cost that grows with it.
The cache a drafter reads can be the target’s own, so could the selection it follows come from the target too?

This is the selection that drafting has wanted and given up: top- k k attention “can achieve very high

cost” ( Sadhukhan et al., 2025 ) .
Verification-guided methods recover it by extracting it from a dense target’s

Our key insight is simple: a natively sparse target has already settled where a drafter’s context should come
from, with its cache and its selection, and paid for both.
One selection also holds across a block: made one step early, for the token just before it, it serves every
slot.
On DS-V4.1-Flash it covers close to nine tenths of what each later token would select, against less than a
fifth for a window of the same size ( Section 3.3 ).

blocks.en:
We present DFly2, a block-parallel drafter that shares the target’s sparsity : the compact KV cache
it maintains and the positions its sparse layers attend to.
Each draft layer reads the KV that a paired target layer has cached ( KV sharing ), at the positions
that layer’s indexer selected, a fixed number drawn from anywhere in the context ( Index sharing ).
DFly2 thus runs no scoring pass and keeps no cache of its own, so it needs no place on the prefill instances,
inherits every prefix-cache hit of the target, and costs no decode concurrency ( Section 4 ).
The selection was made for the target’s queries, yet the drafter is a far smaller model with queries of its
own.
Each draft layer starts from its paired layer’s weights, including the query latent that layer shares with its
indexer, so draft queries begin in the space that produced the selection.
With the target’s last-layer hidden state, which no cache holds, gated into the block, DFly2 reuses four
things the target has already computed: its KV, its selection, its layer weights and that state.
An intra-block correction then rereads the shared context slot by slot.

blocks.en:
We instantiate DFly2 on three targets that differ in their variant of DeepSeek Sparse Attention
(DSA) ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) and in architecture, taking each target’s selection in the form it gives
( Section 4 ).
DS-V4.1-Flash keeps one cache shared across its layers as YOCO does ( Sun et al., 2024b ) , GLM-5.3-Flash interleaves
DSA layers with linear attention ones, and Hy4 flash compresses the index of its sparse layers in two stages
( Section 2 ).
On all three, DFly2 accepts more tokens per step than DFlash and DSpark trained on the same recipe, on every
benchmark and temperature ( Section 5.2 ).
Its margin over the stronger baseline grows from 3.9%–10.5% on general workloads to 10.0%–31.5% on
long-context and agentic ones.
On agentic workloads, whose prompts mostly run longer, its average stays within 4% of its general average,
while DSpark’s falls by 11% to 21%.
The target’s selection reaches anywhere in the context yet stays a fixed size, so DFly2 inherits its length
generalization.
What DFly2 reads is not tuned to a target but taken from it, which is why the same design holds on all three
architectures.
Accepted length turns into speed, and with nothing added at prefill, DFly2 averages a higher end-to-end
speedup than the baselines on every target and workload family ( Section 5.3 ).

blocks.zh: 我们的贡献有三:

blocks.en:
• A drafter can take the target’s selection as it is. A context of the drafter’s own costs more than memory, reaching prefill, prefix caching and decode
concurrency.
Our insight is that the selection it needs is already computed, and paid for, by the target.
We measure how far one selection carries: made one step early, it still covers close to nine tenths of
what each later token in the block would select on DS-V4.1-Flash. • DFly2 shares the target’s selection alongside its cache. DFly2 takes both: each draft layer reads its paired target layer’s KV cache, at the positions that
layer’s indexer selected, and starts from that layer’s weights.
DFly2 therefore keeps no cache, runs no scoring pass, and reads a fixed number of positions from
anywhere in the context, so the costs above do not apply.
We add two pieces: the last-layer state that no cache holds, and an intra-block correction that rereads
the shared context. • Gains that grow with the context, on all three targets. Against baselines trained on the same recipe, DFly2’s margin in accepted length over the stronger one
grows from 3.9%–10.5% on general workloads to 10.0%–31.5% on long-context and agentic ones.
It generalizes past its training length: on agentic workloads its average accepted length stays within
4% of its general average.
Serving at high concurrency on DS-V4.1-Flash, at matched per-user decode speed, it delivers 28% more
throughput on short text and 62% and 81% more on a long-context and an agentic set at 64K.

blocks.en: Owning a cache of its own costs a drafter in three places, and attention over the context adds a fourth cost at every step.

blocks.en:
At prefill, a cache of its own adds compute but mainly constrains where the drafter runs.
Under prefill-decode disaggregation the drafter must also run on the prefill instances, where it holds its
weights, projects an injection at every prompt position and transfers the resulting cache to the decode
instance.
KV sharing adds nothing at prefill, because the latents the drafter reads are ones the target has already written.

权重, 在每个快速位置投出一个注入, 并将生成的缓存转入解码
举个例子。
KV 共享在预填时没有添加任何内容, 因为起草者读取的潜入是目标已经写入的 。

blocks.en:
A cache of its own also leaves the target fewer and shorter prefix-cache hits.
The drafter’s own cache is projected from the target’s hidden states, which prefix caching does not keep.
It must therefore either be kept in the prefix cache or be rebuilt by recomputing the target.
If kept, it takes over two fifths of each cached prefix’s memory on DS-V4.1-Flash
( Table 2 ), so the pool holds fewer prefixes for multi-turn and agentic workloads to reuse.
Rebuilding it shortens the target’s own hit, since the target must recompute the hidden states the hit
would have skipped.
After each hit, vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) recomputes the last 128 tokens to restore the target’s sliding windows on
DS-V4.1-Flash, so a drafter window avoids both only if it is no longer than those 128 tokens.
Under KV sharing the drafter has no cache of its own to keep or rebuild, so every target hit is also a drafter hit.

selection once judged too costly for drafting ( Sadhukhan et al., 2025 ) ( Section 3.2 ).

same size ( Section 3.3 ). Section 4 turns both into mechanisms, KV sharing to read the target’s KV cache and Index sharing to read the positions the target itself selected.

context.

blocks.en:
We evaluate on three natively sparse targets, DS-V4.1-Flash ( DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) , GLM-5.3-Flash ( GLM-5 Team, 2026 ) and Hy4 flash ( Tencent Hy Team, 2026a ) .
Their sparse attention differs in each case ( Section 2 ), so each sets its own paired layers and
top- k k , the near window where it keeps one, and the corresponding number of positions per draft step
( Table 4 ).
Every drafter has three layers of 128 routed experts, 6B to 14B parameters of which 0.4B to 1.1B are
active per token, and reuses the target’s embedding and output head.
The baselines cover both ways of owning a cache ( Section 3.1 ): DFlash ( Chen et al., 2026 ) keeps one
over the whole context, and DSpark ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) bounds its own to a sliding window.
DFlash † is DFlash held to that same window, 128 tokens and 512 on Hy4 flash, which separates
the window from DSpark’s other changes.
We train all three ourselves with the same recipe, data and number of steps as DFly2.
They have the same three-layer MoE stack and come within 2% of its size.
Unless noted otherwise, every number we report is measured on NVIDIA H20 GPUs.

We train on DFly-SFT, a general-purpose instruction-tuning corpus of 989,861 conversations and 7.42B
tokens, all of it from public datasets.
The conversations fall into ten capability domains ( Table 5 ), labeled by their source
where it gives a label and by an LLM annotator otherwise.
Samples are capped at 32,768 tokens, and each domain is filled with its longest samples first, which
makes the mixture long-form and reasoning-heavy.
An explicit reasoning trace appears in 61.6% of samples and 34.9% run past 8K tokens, so a drafter
meets long contexts during training.
The corpus is deduplicated globally and decontaminated against the twelve DeepSpec evaluation
sets ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) with an n-gram overlap test.

Of the two things the drafter shares, accepted length comes from the selection, whose scoring pass over
every position the target has already run ( Tables 10 and 3.2 ).
Removing its top- k k leaves only the near window, the largest loss here and two to six times as costly
on the long-context family as on the general-purpose one.
A window chooses by position, and the longer the context, the more it misses.
The near window itself is worth about 3% on DS-V4.1-Flash and nothing on the other two.
On DS-V4.1-Flash the indexer scores one set of latents shared across layers, while each layer also
caches its own for the most recent 128 positions, which the top- k k cannot reach ( Section 4 ).
A drafter with its own cache over that same near window accepts at most 3% more on GLM-5.3-Flash and
Hy4 flash.
Sharing the cache therefore affects accepted length only slightly while removing the three costs of Section 3.1 .
Because the drafter reads the selection as each target makes it, how much each term adds follows the
target’s structure, and one design serves all three with nothing to tune in what it reads
( Section 4 ).

blocks.en:
DS-V4.1-Flash follows YOCO ( Sun et al., 2024b ) in keeping one set of latents that all layers share, and the
drafter reads that same cache.
Every indexer of the target therefore selects over what the drafter reads, which opens a design space in
how the drafter picks its top- k k .
We explore three dimensions, earlier rows, more layers and a larger budget per row, and score each read
by its top- k k mass recall ( Figure 8 ).
All three start from DFly2’s own read, the target’s top-512 at the row before the anchor, which on
average already recalls 0.80 of each slot’s own top-512 by index score.
Adding two earlier rows reaches 0.86 at under 1K positions, the union of the target’s five indexers
0.85 at 1.4K, and a 2K budget per row 0.89.
Earlier rows thus gain the most recall per added position, about twice the other two, and combining them
with the union reaches 0.91 at 2.6K positions.
Each read stays cheap, as 2K positions add 0.19% to a decode step, against 14% to 23% for the whole
context at 128K ( Section 3.1 ).

blocks.en: 6 Related Work
blocks.zh: 6 相关工作

blocks.en:
Block-parallel drafters build a context KV of their own that spans the prompt and grows with it.
DFlash ( Chen et al., 2026 ) fuses hidden states from several target layers, injects them into every draft layer
as extra keys and values, and drafts a whole block in one forward pass.
Its successors refine the conditioning signal ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ) or model the dependency between
slots ( Cheng et al., 2026 ; Rheinboldt et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) , and DFly ( Liu et al., 2026a ) does both.
All of them keep this cache, and their intra-block corrections do not return to the context.
DLite ( Xu et al., 2026 ) avoids the cost by keeping no cache at all and conditioning on hidden states from many
target layers at the latest position.
DFly2 also builds no context KV of its own, but it still reads the context through the target’s cache,
and so does its intra-block correction.
blocks.zh:
块相平行的起草者建立他们自己的上下文KV,这个上下文跨越了快取并随它而增长.
DFlash (Chen等, 2026年) 从多个目标地层中导出隐形状态, 注入到每个抽取地层中
作为额外的密钥和值,并在一个前传中起草一个整块.
其后继者精炼了调节信号(Zhang等,2026;Lin等,2026)或模拟了两者之间的依赖关系.

H-Spec ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) reads a fixed window, and LongSpark ( He et al., 2026 ) reads a recent window plus a
summary pooled by fixed queries.
All of them were developed on dense targets, which attend to every position and so offer no selection to
follow.
DFly2 also reads the target’s cache, but at the positions a natively sparse target attends to.

blocks.en:
Query-aware selection gives good drafts, but prior work either finds it too costly for drafting or extracts
it from a dense target’s attention.
TriForce ( Sun et al., 2024a ) drafts from a cache retrieved by the current query, whereas
MagicDec ( Sadhukhan et al., 2025 ) finds per-query search too costly at large batch sizes and drafts from a static
sparse cache.
Verification-guided methods read the selection off the target’s attention during verification.
Either the target itself then drafts ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Yue et al., 2026 ) , or a separate drafter keeps a cache of its own
and reads only the chunks the target ranks highest ( Cha et al., 2025 ) .
In every case, the drafting side has to compute or extract the selection itself.

blocks.en:
Natively sparse targets such as DeepSeek-V3.2, DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-5 compute a query-aware selection as part
of their own attention ( Yuan et al., 2025 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ; GLM-5 Team, 2026 ) , and within a model one selection can already
serve several layers ( Bai et al., 2026 ) .
Systems work on these targets speeds up the target’s side of speculative decoding, through sparse
verification kernels ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , indexer prediction ( Fu et al., 2026 ) and tree verification over compressed
attention ( Liu and Li, 2026 ) .
The drafters paired with these targets, however, still bring a context of their own: the MTP modules shipped
with these models keep their own KV cache ( GLM-5 Team, 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) , and DSpark serves DeepSeek-V4 with its own
128-token window ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) .
GLM-5.2 goes as far as reusing a selection across draft steps, but the selection is its MTP module’s
own. 3 3 3 Enabled by index_share_for_mtp_iteration in the released GLM-5.2 configuration
( https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.2 ). The sharing mechanism follows IndexCache ( Bai et al., 2026 ) . To our knowledge, no prior drafter reuses the target’s own selection.
DFly2 reuses both the target’s cache and its selection, so the drafter keeps no cache and computes no
selection of its own.

blocks.en: 7 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 7 结论

blocks.en:
Long contexts have turned targets natively sparse, and speculative decoding increasingly runs on them.
Their drafters still bring a context of their own, a cache that costs more than the memory it takes,
read at positions a rule fixed before the query arrives.
A natively sparse target picks positions for each query already, over a cache it keeps anyway, and has
paid for both.
DFly2 shares both, reading each paired target layer’s cached KV ( KV sharing ) at the positions
that layer’s indexer selected ( Index sharing ).
It stores nothing per context position, scores nothing, and reads the same number of positions at any
prompt length.

blocks.en:
On three targets whose sparse attention and architecture differ, DFly2 accepts more tokens per step
than DFlash and DSpark trained on the same recipe.
Its margin over the stronger one widens from 3.9%–10.5% on general workloads to 10.0%–31.5% on
long-context and agentic workloads of up to 128K.
At high concurrency on DS-V4.1-Flash, at matched per-user decode speed, that becomes 62% and 81% more
throughput at 64K.
The gain grows with the context because what DFly2 reads does not, the target’s selection being a fixed
size that can still fall anywhere.
Long contexts are where serving needs speculative decoding most, and they are where following the
target’s own choices pays most.
